questions.question: An administrator must ensure that users without the itil role cannot read Priority 1 Incident records, whether they open a list, a form, or call a web service API. What should be configured?

options.text: A UI policy on the Incident form
A role on the Incidents application module
A read ACL on the Incident table
A data policy on the Incident table

explanation.correct: Access control lists restrict access to data by requiring users to pass a set of requirements before they can interact with it. A read ACL on the incident table can require a role and use the Applies To filter to target only Priority 1 records. Failing a read ACL hides the records in lists and forms and also blocks retrieval through web service APIs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI policies only apply to data entered on a form through the standard browser, so they cannot stop users from reading records in lists or through web service APIs.
Applications and modules list the roles required to view them, so a module role only controls who sees the module. Record and field access is secured by ACL rules, not by roles on modules.
Data policies enforce data consistency by setting mandatory and read-only states for fields. They do not decide which users may read a record.

source.excerpt: Most security settings are implemented using access controls. In addition to restricting CRUD operations, access control rules can restrict ServiceNow specific operations on tables and fields.

questions.question: An administrator can open and debug ACL records but cannot create a new ACL or save changes to an existing one. Which role must they elevate to in their session?

options.text: user_admin
security_admin
impersonator
role_delegator

explanation.correct: Normal admin users can view and debug access control rules, but creating or updating ACLs requires elevating privileges to the security_admin role. In the base system security_admin is the only elevated privilege role, and it lasts only for the current session, which is why the admin must elevate before editing. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: user_admin is a user administration role; the docs note it cannot even grant the admin role. Creating or changing ACLs specifically requires the elevated security_admin role.
The impersonator role is what lets a user impersonate other users. It does not grant the right to create or update access control rules.
role_delegator lets a user assign the roles they hold to members of a group. It has nothing to do with editing ACL records, which requires security_admin.

source.excerpt: In the base system, only the default system administrator has the security admin role. Others with the admin role must also be granted the security admin role to manage ACLs.

questions.question: An administrator elevated to security_admin yesterday to update ACLs, then logged out at the end of the day. After logging back in today, what is the status of that elevated role?

options.text: It stays active until deselected in the Elevate Roles dialog
It ended with the session, so the admin must elevate again
It is now saved as a permanent role on the admin's user record
It returns automatically because the admin role contains it

explanation.correct: An elevated privilege role lasts only for the duration of the user session; a session timeout or logout removes it. Users do not have elevated roles on login and must manually elevate again. Because the admin logged out yesterday, the security_admin elevation ended and must be re-selected through Elevate Roles before editing ACLs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Deselecting in the dialog is one way to end elevation, but logout also terminates elevated privileges with the session, so nothing is still active today.
Elevation never becomes a permanent assignment. By default users do not have elevated privilege roles upon login and must manually elevate each session.
The Security Administrator role is not inherited by the admin role, and an elevated role must be manually elevated even when another role contains it.

source.excerpt: Elevated roles allow modification of the access control list. These roles last only for your session. They end with logout, session time out, or user impersonation.

questions.question: A security administrator adds a Deny-Unless read ACL to a custom table that already has an Allow-If read ACL. When a user requests a record from that table, how are the two decision types evaluated?

options.text: Allow-If first; a passing Allow-If ACL skips the Deny-Unless
The ACL that was created most recently is evaluated first
Deny-Unless first; if it fails, access is denied outright
Deny-Unless first; if it passes, access is granted outright

explanation.correct: Deny-Unless ACLs take priority over Allow-If ACLs because they are evaluated first. A Deny-Unless ACL denies access unless its roles, conditions, security attributes and script are met; if it fails, access is denied. If it passes, evaluation continues, and because an Allow-If ACL also matches, that Allow-If ACL must still permit access. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/acl-denial-behavior.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The order is the reverse: Deny-Unless ACLs are evaluated first and take priority, so a passing Allow-If ACL cannot bypass a failing Deny-Unless ACL.
Evaluation priority comes from the decision type, not from when the ACL was created. Deny-Unless ACLs are evaluated before Allow-If ACLs.
A passing Deny-Unless ACL only lets evaluation proceed. When an Allow-If ACL also matches, access is granted only if that Allow-If ACL explicitly permits it.

source.excerpt: The system checks deny rules first. If any deny rules conditions are unmet, access is blocked, requiring all matching deny rule conditions to be satisfied for access to proceed.

questions.question: An administrator is creating a custom table in System Definition > Tables and wants basic security rules generated for it, along with a role that users need to access the table. What should they do on the table form?

options.text: Select the Extensible check box in the Controls section
Select Create access controls and enter a User role
Set Accessible from to This application scope only
Clear Allow access to this table via web services

explanation.correct: On the table form, the Create access controls check box creates basic security rules for the new table. Once it is selected, the User role field becomes available so the administrator can enter a new role name or pick an existing role that is required to access the table. This produces the ACLs and role in one step. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/table-administration-and-data-management/t_CreateATable.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Extensible only controls whether other tables are allowed to extend this table. It does not create any security rules or access roles.
Accessible from defines which application scopes can access the table. It is an application access setting and does not generate ACLs for users.
Clearing this check box prevents inbound web service queries to the table. It does not create the basic security rules or a required role.

source.excerpt: With system created access controls, it is rare to have a table with no access control rules. When a table is created, access controls are automatically created.

questions.question: An ITIL user passes the table-level read ACL on the Incident table but fails the field-level read ACL on one Incident field. What does the user see when opening an incident?

options.text: The full record, including that field
Nothing, because the whole record is denied
The record, with that one field hidden
The record, with that field shown read-only

explanation.correct: For record ACLs, the matching table-level and field-level ACLs must both evaluate to true for the field, so passing the table ACL lets the user open the record while the failed field read ACL removes that field. The docs state that failing a read ACL prevents the user from seeing the object and, depending on the object, "hides a field on a form". See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The failed field-level read ACL still applies: for record ACLs the table-level and field-level ACLs must both evaluate to true, so the field is not shown.
The user passed the table-level read ACL, so the record itself is readable; the failed field ACL only affects that field, which a failed read ACL hides on the form.
A read-only field is the documented result of failing a write ACL. Failing a read ACL means the user can't see the object in forms or lists.

source.excerpt: Access controls are checked in order, starting with table access and then field access. Failing a table rule denies access to all passing a table rule, but failing a field rule denies access to that field.

questions.question: An administrator creates a custom table without table-specific ACLs, so its records match just the wild-card (*) table ACLs. With glide.sm.default_mode set to Deny access, who can access those records?

options.text: Any authenticated user
Users with the admin role
No users, admins included
Users with the table's role

explanation.correct: The base system has wild-card table rules (*) for the create, read, write, and delete operations. The Security manager default behavior property (glide.sm.default_mode) decides whether users can access objects that only match these wild-card table ACLs: "When this property is set to Deny access, only administrators can access objects that match the wild-card table ACLs." That is why the docs advise creating ACLs when you create a table unless you want to use the wild-card ACLs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: With glide.sm.default_mode set to Deny access, objects that only match the wild-card table ACLs are restricted to administrators, so ordinary logged-in users are denied.
The property doesn't lock out everyone: when it is set to Deny access, administrators can still access objects that match only the wild-card table ACLs.
A role created for the table doesn't help here, because no table-specific ACL references it. The records match just the wild-card ACLs, which the Deny access setting restricts to administrators.

source.excerpt: ACL rules for parent tables apply to their child tables.

questions.question: An administrator adds the itil role to an agent who is currently logged in, but the agent still can't open records that the role should allow. What should the agent do?

options.text: Log out and back in to start a new session
Elevate to the security_admin role
Ask to have the role added to a group as well
Ask a role delegator to assign the role again

explanation.correct: A newly assigned role does not apply to a session that is already running. The docs state: "Whenever a user is assigned a new role, it only takes effect after logging in with a new session", and "If the user is logged in when you update their roles and they’re unable to access records enabled by the new role, they may need to log out and back in again." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_AssignARoleToAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: security_admin is an elevated role that provides access to ACLs and High Security Settings. Elevating to it doesn't apply a newly assigned itil role to the current session.
Roles from groups and directly assigned roles behave the same way here. Any newly assigned role only takes effect after the user logs in with a new session.
The role is already assigned. Having a role delegator assign it again doesn't change the fact that new roles only take effect in a new session.

source.excerpt: System administrators typically use three security modules-- security, ACL list, and high security settings.

questions.question: An administrator who doesn't have the Security Incident Response roles impersonates a user who is a Security Incident Response admin. What should the administrator expect during the session?

options.text: Full access to security incidents, like the impersonated user
Limited access to security incidents and some modules
Their own menus and roles stay in effect throughout
The ability to change that user's password afterward

explanation.correct: Impersonating a user with an application-specific admin role is restricted. The docs state: "Impersonating a user with an application-specific admin role, like Human Resources admin or Security Incident Response, limits access to certain features such as security incidents and profile information, unless these roles are already assigned to the impersonating admin. This restriction extends to certain modules and applications in the navigation bar." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/c_ImpersonateAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Access is limited, not full. Features such as security incidents stay restricted unless the impersonating admin already has those roles.
Impersonation lets the administrator access the system exactly as the impersonated user, including identical menus and modules, so their own menus don't stay in effect.
The docs state that admins can't change the password of users with application admin roles.

source.excerpt: However, admins cannot impersonate the security admin role or elevate privileges during impersonation to access high security functions.

questions.question: A security administrator is cleaning up ACLs. Under the ACL engine's deny-by-default behavior, which two ACLs are treated as invalid, so access is denied? (Choose two)

options.text: An ACL whose only required role doesn't exist
An ACL with Applies-to set to Priority 1 records
An ACL whose script just contains answer=true
An ACL that pairs the itil role with a data condition

explanation.correct: "By default the ACL engine completely denies access if an ACL is empty or invalid." The docs define invalid ACLs as "ACLs with roles that do not exist", ACLs with security attributes that do not exist, and "ACLs with a script that contains 'answer=true' or 'true'". Access is denied when none of the roles that an ACL references exist on the instance. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Applies-to is a valid way to control which records an ACL applies to (for example, only Priority 1 incidents). It doesn't make the ACL empty or invalid.
Requiring a role and adding a data condition are normal ACL conditions. A user must pass all of them, but the ACL is valid.

source.excerpt: ServiceNow ensures security for CRUD operations with, user authentication/login, managed via users, groups and roles, application and module access controlled by roles.

questions.question: While impersonating an ITIL user to reproduce a reported problem, an administrator adds a work note to an incident. How is that update recorded?

options.text: As performed by the administrator's own account
As performed by the impersonated ITIL user
As performed by the system user, not a person
It isn't saved, because impersonation is read-only

explanation.correct: Impersonation, which is primarily used for testing, lets the administrator access the system exactly as the impersonated user. The docs state: "All actions performed by the administrator during impersonation are recorded as if they were executed by the impersonated user." The start and end of the impersonation are logged separately in the system log as Impersonate Begin and Impersonate End events. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/c_ImpersonateAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Actions taken during impersonation are recorded as if the impersonated user performed them, not under the administrator's account. Only the start and end of impersonation are logged separately, as the Impersonate Begin and Impersonate End events in the system log.
The docs say impersonated actions are recorded as executed by the impersonated user, not by a system account.
Impersonation isn't read-only. The administrator accesses the system exactly as the user, and their actions are recorded as that user's.

source.excerpt: Impersonation allows administrators to test and troubleshoot by viewing the platform as another user would see it.

questions.question: An itil user reports that the System Definition application doesn't appear in her application navigator. What controls whether an application or module is shown to a user?

options.text: The roles listed on the application or module
Roles added to the table's dictionary entry
Read ACLs on the fields of the module's table
UI policies on the application menu's form

explanation.correct: "Applications and modules contain lists of the roles required to view them. For example, to view the System Definition application, the admin role is required. Security rights for applications and modules are still defined using role arrays." ACLs secure tables and fields, but navigator visibility comes from these role lists. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/r_ContextualSecurity.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Under the Contextual Security Manager, roles on dictionary entries are no longer tested. Adding them doesn't change any rights.
ACLs secure table and field data. Application and module visibility is defined with role arrays on the application and module.
UI policies only apply to data entered on a form through the standard browser. They don't control which applications appear in the navigator.

source.excerpt: A user needs BOTH a role AND ACL access to see data. Roles grant access to application modules, while ACLs control record-level access.

questions.question: The System Administrator wants to give a colleague the security_admin role so she can maintain ACLs. What must the System Administrator do to grant it?

options.text: Elevate to security_admin, then assign it
Grant her the admin role, which contains it
Ask a user_admin to add it to her user record
Have her elevate to security_admin on her own

explanation.correct: "To grant the security_admin role to a user, the granting user must also have the admin role and must elevate to the security_admin role before granting the security_admin role to other users. A user with only the admin role cannot grant the security_admin role to other users." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_AssignARoleToAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The Security Administrator role is not inherited by the admin role and must be explicitly assigned, so granting admin doesn't grant security_admin.
The granting user must have the admin role and be elevated to security_admin. A user with only user_admin can't even grant the admin role.
To use an elevated role, it must be assigned to you first. She can't elevate to security_admin until someone grants it to her.

source.excerpt: Elevated roles allow modification of the access control list. These roles last only for your session.

questions.question: An IT manager asks for the admin role so she can maintain a few catalog items. Which two statements about the admin role are accurate? (Choose two)

options.text: It can override ACL rules and pass all role checks
It can create ACLs without elevating to security_admin
Avoid assigning it when a more targeted role exists
The admin role contains the security_admin role

explanation.correct: The base system roles reference describes admin as having "access to all system features, functions, and data because administrators can override access control list (ACL) rules and pass all role checks. Avoid assigning this role to your users when more targeted roles are available." For this request, catalog_admin is a more targeted role. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/r_BaseSystemRoles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Normal admin users can view and debug ACLs, but to create or update them administrators must elevate to the security_admin role.
The Security Administrator role is not inherited by the admin role and must be explicitly assigned.

source.excerpt: Admins have access to all platform features and can override access controls so assign this role cautiously.

questions.question: A service desk is onboarding 40 agents who all need the same set of roles. Which approach does ServiceNow recommend to keep user administration simple?

options.text: Add the roles to each agent's own user record
Assign the roles to a group and add the agents
Grant every agent the admin role to cover all
Make one agent a role delegator for the others

explanation.correct: Users inherit roles from all groups they belong to. The docs advise: "When possible, simplify user administration by assigning roles to groups. Create groups that contain all the roles necessary for specific personas, and then assign users to those groups." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_AssignARoleToAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Roles can be assigned directly to users, but the docs recommend assigning roles to persona groups to simplify user administration.
admin gives access to all system features and data. The docs say to avoid assigning it when more targeted roles are available.
Role delegators can only assign roles they already have, within groups. This doesn't replace persona groups for granting a standard role set.

questions.question: An administrator creates elevated role A, which contains elevated role B, and assigns both to an analyst. The analyst elevates to role A only. What is true for her session?

options.text: She gets role B's privileges through role A
She must still elevate to role B to use it
Role B elevates by itself at her next login
She keeps both roles after she logs out

explanation.correct: To use an elevated role, "You must manually elevate to a specific elevated role to get its privileges, even if you are already elevated to a second elevated role that contains the first elevated role. For example, if elevated role A contains elevated role B, even if you elevate to role A, you must still elevate to role B to get its privileges." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/c_ElevatedPrivilege.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Containment doesn't carry elevated privileges. Each elevated role must be elevated to manually, even when it is contained in a role that is already elevated.
"By default, you do not have elevated privilege roles upon login. You must manually elevate to the privilege of the role."
An elevated privilege role lasts only for the user session. Session timeout or logout removes the role.

questions.question: A new employee uses the Self-Service application to get help from IT. Which two actions does Self-Service give access to by default? (Choose two)

options.text: Accessing the Service Catalog
Creating access control rules
Viewing knowledge articles
Administering users and groups

explanation.correct: "By default, the Self-Service application provides access to common actions, such as viewing your homepage, accessing the Service Catalog, viewing knowledge articles, working with incidents, and taking surveys." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/servicenow-platform/self-service/r_EmployeeSelfService.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Creating or updating ACLs is not a self-service action. Administrators must elevate to the security_admin role to create or update access control rules.
Administering users, groups, locations, skills, and companies is what the user_admin role is for. It is not a default self-service action.

questions.question: A QA lead is given the impersonator role so she can test forms as other users. Which statement describes what the role allows her to do?

options.text: Impersonate users, but not users with admin
Impersonate any user, including admin users
Impersonate only members of her own groups
Impersonate users only after elevating first

explanation.correct: The base system roles reference says "Impersonators can impersonate users" and warns: "This role doesn’t enable the impersonation of admin users." The impersonate-a-user procedure lists impersonator as the required role. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/r_BaseSystemRoles.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_ImpersonateAUserInUI16.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: The docs warn that the impersonator role doesn't enable the impersonation of admin users.
The role description, "Impersonators can impersonate users", sets no group-membership limit. The documented restriction is on admin users.
impersonator isn't an elevated role. In the base system, security_admin is the only role with elevated privileges. The procedure only requires the impersonator role.

questions.question: An administrator grants a catalog manager the catalog_admin role. What does this base system role allow her to do?

options.text: Manage catalog categories and items in Service Catalog
Create and publish items only within assigned categories
Administer users, groups, locations, skills, and companies
Delete incidents, problems, changes, and related records

explanation.correct: "Catalog administrators can manage the Service Catalog application, including catalog categories and items." catalog_admin contains user_criteria_admin, catalog_builder_editor, catalog_template_editor, catalog, and catalog_lookup_admin. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/r_BaseSystemRoles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: That is the catalog_editor role, whose users "can create, modify, and publish items within categories that they’re assigned to".
That is the user_admin role: "User administrators can administer users, groups, locations, skills, and companies."
That is the itil_admin role, whose users "can delete incidents, problems, changes, and other related records".

questions.question: A security administrator wants one place to view the instance's hardening compliance score, the top non-compliant hardening settings, and the results of security scans. Which application should they use?

options.text: Contextual Security Manager
ServiceNow Security Center
Instance Security Center
High Security Settings

explanation.correct: Security Center is a free application, installed by default since the Vancouver release, that helps organizations maintain the security of their ServiceNow deployments. Its security configuration console shows the hardening compliance score, trends, the top non-compliant hardening settings and security scan results, which matches every need in this scenario. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/security-center/sec-center-v2.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Contextual Security Manager controls read, write, create and delete authorization through ACL rules. It does not provide compliance scores or scan results.
Instance Security Center reached end of sales in September 2024 and is no longer supported or available for activation; Security Center replaces it.
High Security Settings is a set of security properties and features such as the security_admin role and default deny, not a dashboard of compliance and scan results.

questions.question: Users with the itil role must still see the Priority field on incidents but must not be able to change it in forms, lists, or web service calls. What should a security administrator create?

options.text: A write ACL on incident.priority that itil users fail
A read ACL on incident.priority that itil users fail
A list_edit ACL on the incident table that itil users fail
A UI policy that locks the Priority field for itil users

explanation.correct: Failing a write ACL means the "User sees a read-only field in forms and lists, and the user can’t update records using API protocols such as web services." A field-level write ACL on incident.priority that itil users can't pass keeps the field visible but read-only everywhere. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Failing a read ACL means the user can't see the object in forms or lists, so Priority would be hidden instead of read-only.
Failing a list_edit ACL only stops users from updating records from a list. Forms and web services would still allow changes.
UI policies only apply to data entered on a form through the standard browser, so lists and web service calls would not be restricted.

questions.question: A new security administrator is reviewing how ACLs are defined. Which three things does every access control list (ACL) specify? (Choose three)

options.text: The object being secured, like a table or field
The decision type and the operation, such as read
The conditions, such as roles and data conditions
The update set that captured the ACL record
The UI policy applied to the table's form

explanation.correct: "All access control lists specify: The decision type, rule type and operation which defines the ACL; The object being secured; The conditions required to access the object." Conditions can include required roles, security attributes, data conditions, and a script. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: An update set isn't one of the components every ACL specifies. The components are the decision type and operation, the object, and the conditions.
UI policies are separate from ACLs and only apply to data entered on a form through the standard browser. They aren't part of an ACL definition.

questions.question: A security administrator notices two Allow-If read ACLs on the incident.number field at the same point in the processing order. A user passes one of them and fails the other. What happens?

options.text: The user can read the field, since passing one is enough
Access is denied because every matching ACL must be passed
Only the older ACL is evaluated and the newer one is ignored
The more restrictive ACL wins, so the field is hidden

explanation.correct: When two or more ACLs match at the same point in the processing order, the user only has to pass any one of them. The docs use this exact example: with two field ACLs on incident.number, a user who passes one rule can access the number field even if they fail the other. The all-must-pass rule applies only to multiple Deny-Unless ACLs. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/access-control/exploring-access-control-list.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Requiring every matching ACL to pass is the behavior for multiple Deny-Unless ACLs on a resource. For Allow-If ACLs at the same point, passing any one is enough.
Both ACLs are considered. If two or more ACLs match at the same point in the processing order, passing any one of them grants access.
There is no most-restrictive-wins rule for Allow-If ACLs at the same processing point; a user who passes one of them has access to the field.

questions.question: A service desk team lead must be able to delete duplicate incident records. Which base system role is intended for team leads and grants this?

options.text: The itil role
The itil_admin role
The snc_read_only role
The catalog_admin role

explanation.correct: "ITIL administrators can delete incidents, problems, changes, and other related records. This role is intended for team leads." The itil role is the base system technician role, used to open, update, and close incidents, problems, and changes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/r_BaseSystemRoles.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: itil is the base system technician role. Its description covers opening, updating, and closing incidents, problems, and changes. Deleting them is what itil_admin is described as granting.
Users with snc_read_only can't insert, update, or delete records, whatever other roles they have.
catalog_admin is for managing the Service Catalog application, including catalog categories and items, not for deleting incidents.

questions.question: A user in the Paris office opens User Menu > Preferences > Language & Region to switch the interface to French, but there is no Language option. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Her Country preference hasn't been set
No other language plugin is installed
Dynamic Translation isn't enabled yet
Her date format is still the default

explanation.correct: The Language preference "Sets the language used for your instance when you have access to more than one language. This preference displays only when another language plugin is installed." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-user-interface/next-experience-language-preferences.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Country sets the country code and, combined with a language, the user locale for currency and number formatting. It doesn't control whether the Language option appears.
Dynamic Translation provides on-demand machine translation of content such as form fields, chat messages, and knowledge articles. It doesn't add Language to the preferences.
Date format only sets how dates display, and it updates the Combined date and time format choices. It doesn't affect the Language option.

questions.question: A group manager is designated as a role delegator by an administrator and wants to update her team's access. Which action can she now perform?

options.text: Assign roles she holds to members of a group
Assign the admin role to any member of her group
Delegate her role_delegator role to another member
Grant any role in the instance to her group members

explanation.correct: Role delegators are users that administrators allow to assign roles within groups, but they can only assign roles that they already have. On the Delegate Roles in Group form, the roles available for delegating are only the roles the role_delegator has, and the docs note delegators can assign roles inherited from a group as well as roles an administrator assigned to them. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/c_DelegateRoles.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_RoleDelegation.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: By default the admin role cannot be delegated, so a role delegator cannot hand it out even to members of a group she manages.
A user with the role_delegator role can't delegate that role to other group members; role_delegator is non-delegable by default.
Delegators are limited to roles they already hold; the Roles to delegate list only offers roles that the role_delegator has.

questions.question: An administrator opens a user record to remove the itil role, but the user received that role from the Service Desk group. What must the administrator do?

options.text: Delete the itil row from the user's Roles list
Remove the user from the Service Desk group
Elevate to security_admin, then delete the row
Assign snc_read_only to cancel out the itil role

explanation.correct: A user inherits roles from all groups they belong to. The docs state: "You can't delete roles that are assigned to the group from the user record. You must remove the user from the group record." See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-administration/user-administration/t_AssignARoleToAUser.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Roles that come from a group can't be deleted from the user record. The user must be removed from the group.
security_admin is for ACLs and High Security Settings. The docs don't offer elevation as a way around this; group-assigned roles must be removed through the group record.
snc_read_only complements a user's other roles by blocking insert, update, and delete. It doesn't remove the itil role.

questions.question: An administrator on a new instance confirms that the High Security Settings plugin is active and wants to know what it provides. Which capability is part of High Security Settings?

options.text: An elevated security_admin role for changing ACLs
Automatic encryption of the tables in the database
Multi-factor authentication enforced at user login
Blocking of inbound SOAP and CSV web service requests

explanation.correct: High Security Settings, active by default on new instances, provides a Security Administrator role, elevated privileges, a default deny property, property access controls and ACLs. The plugin separates user functionality from access control management by requiring administrators to explicitly elevate into security_admin before making access control changes. See https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/exploring-high-security-settings.html and https://www.servicenow.com/docs/r/platform-security/instance-security-hardening-settings/sc-high-security-plugin.html

wrongAnswers.explanation: Database encryption is not among the High Security Settings features, which cover default properties, default deny, the security_admin role, elevated privileges and ACLs.
Multi-factor authentication is not one of the features delivered by High Security Settings; the plugin focuses on access control and hardened properties.
High Security Settings properties require authorization for inbound SOAP and CSV requests rather than blocking them outright.
